Smart DIY vehicle mechanics is knowing when you give it to a pro to do.

I weigh hiring a pro against three things:

  1. How much would it cost for me to do it myself including time learning? If the time learning is way too high or there's enough of a chance that safety is compromised or I'll have a high learning curve that makes it too much of a time sink, I'll pay someone else to do it.

  2. If the cost of getting tools is prohibitively expensive considering the cost of the tools versus the number of times I'll use those tools, I'll hire someone.

  3. How much would it cost to hire someone versus the time it would take for me to do it? If it would be cheaper to hire someone compared to my current pay rate at work, I hire someone. For example, I have a maid that comes in occasionally to clean my house because she can get it done in two hours whereas I'd have 2 hours to clean, arranging the time block, and the benefit of getting other things done. And sometimes she does it while I'm at while is a 100% time saver. And she does it for $25. You'd have to just about be working fast food for that deal to not make sense.

For example, I can do a tune up on my car and have the tools. I can do an oil change on my truck but I don't have the tools. Once or twice of changing the oil on the truck while I'm gathering the tools is fine to take it into the shop. After that, I'm wasting money. Or a shed I built out of scrap lumber. I could learn the basics to do it myself and hang siding and putting roofing shingles on or I could hire someone for $500+. All I needed to get was one tool for the siding but I had all of the materials otherwise. I took several weeks in my spare time and did it myself. It's not going to pass any building code inspections but it doesn't need to. It just needs to not collapse.

A lot of pros also don't mind if you watch what they're doing because of curiosity or learning that one trick that keeps you from doing it yourself. So it's a learning experience there too if you take it into a pro.

Changing oil, everyone should have those tools as a basic. Strap wrench, adjustable wrench (worst case scenario), and a drain pan. Warm up the engine, undo the drain plug, let all the oil drain into the pan, pull the oil filter and replace with new one, put drain plug back in, and fill 'er up. Don't even need a lift or anything if it's a truck, just crawl under there.

Hell, I used to use cut-off milk jugs as my drain pan - and stored the rest in old milk jugs before taking it to the oil dropoff @ the recycling center. There's 0 excuse for not having the tools for an oil change.
